# The Art of Game Design: A Book of Lenses — Jesse Schell

- Type: LINK ONLY card (commercial book; © the author/publisher).
- Source: Jesse Schell, *The Art of Game Design: A Book of Lenses* (2008; 2nd ed. 2015; 3rd ed. 2020). It appears in the open "Video Game Design" bibliography: https://datafield.dev/video-game-design/appendices/bibliography.html
- Author: Jesse Schell — designer (Disney Imagineering VR, Schell Games) and CMU professor; the book is a standard course text.

## The reasoning method, distilled

- **Design by lenses: each lens is one sharp question you interrogate the design with**, in writing, one at a time — e.g. the Lens of Goals (what is the player trying to achieve, and is it clear at every moment?), the Lens of Surprise (where are the deliberate surprises, and are any mechanics surprising *by accident*?), the Lens of the Core Loop (what does the player do every 30 seconds, and why is it satisfying the 100th time?), the Lens of the Problem Statement (what problem is this feature solving, for whom?).
- **The Elemental Tetrad**: mechanics, story, aesthetics (presentation), and technology are four supports of one design; none is "the game" by itself, and a weakness in any one caps the others. A system that exists only as menu text has failed the aesthetics leg.
- The practical habit: when a proposal feels mushy, don't argue — pick the 2–3 lenses that bite hardest on it and answer them in writing. Mush usually means one leg of the tetrad is missing.

## For みゅけ

Our canon already enforces the tetrad's aesthetics leg ("if it isn't on the strip, it isn't shipped"). The lenses worth keeping pinned for proposals: Core Loop, Goals, Surprise, Problem Statement.
